planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions from nursery-propagated stock in early spring or in fall after dormancy, in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil that stays moist through spring; siting near a woodland streambank mimics its wild habitat best.

directions: Site this Pacific Northwest native in dappled shade beneath deciduous cover or along stream-bank woodland where soil is consistently damp in early spring but dries out by summer. Its most distinctive feature is the unusually long petiole that suspends the maroon-brown, nodding flower well below the leaf whorl, unlike the erect blooms of most eastern trilliums. Plants emerge and flower very early, often while snowmelt is still running nearby, then go fully dormant by midsummer. Never dig from the wild; source only nursery-grown divisions, as populations in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington are localized and slow to recover from disturbance.
sources: Idaho Fish and Game Species Catalog

planting.note: Plant divisions of nursery-propagated rhizomes in fall or early spring in humus-rich soil under oak or mixed evergreen woodland; established plants tolerate the dry summers typical of California's Mediterranean climate once dormant.

directions: Endemic to Sierra Nevada foothill and Coast Range woodlands, this sessile trillium holds its slender, faintly musky-scented maroon-purple petals upright directly above a whorl of handsomely mottled leaves, distinguishing it from the broader-petaled Trillium chloropetalum it's often confused with. It thrives in the leaf litter of oak-madrone and mixed conifer woods where winter-spring rains keep the soil moist and summer dormancy is expected. Give it a shaded, undisturbed spot and leave the foliage in place until it yellows naturally to recharge the rhizome for next year's bloom.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, moist, well-drained soil under deciduous cover in a ravine or bluff-like setting; this coastal-plain species tolerates warmer, more humid conditions than most sessile trilliums.

directions: Native to rich alluvial woods and bluffs along the Chattahoochee River drainage of Georgia, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle, this is one of the largest and most vigorous of the sessile, mottled-leaf trilliums, sending up a single erect, deep maroon-purple flower directly atop three broadly patterned leaves. It prefers warm, humid Deep South woodland conditions and rich, well-drained alluvial soil, doing best in partial to full shade beneath hardwoods. Foliage and flower emerge and fade earlier in the season than northern trillium relatives, so mark the planting spot to avoid disturbing the dormant rhizome later in the year.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in rich, well-drained cove-forest soil under deciduous canopy; give it the same siting as its close relative Trillium cuneatum, but expect earlier bloom and noticeably taller flowering stems.

directions: Restricted to rich forests of the Lookout Mountain region where Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama meet, this sessile trillium was long overlooked as an unusual population of Trillium cuneatum before botanists recognized it as a distinct species, formally described only in recent years. It stands noticeably taller than its cuneatum cousin, with longer, more blunt-tipped maroon to bronze petals held above three broadly mottled leaves, and it tends to flower earlier in the season. Plant it in humus-rich, well-drained cove-forest soil in dense to dappled shade, and allow the plant to die back naturally in early summer without cutting the foliage.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in a spot that stays wet through winter and spring but drains and dries by summer; this rare species naturally grows on serpentine soils, so it tolerates lean, mineral-heavy ground better than richer garden loam.

directions: Endemic to a small area of southwestern Oregon's Illinois River valley, where it grows in wet, serpentine-influenced meadows and woodland edges, this camas produces loose racemes of pale to deep violet-blue star-shaped flowers in late spring. It is a good choice for a seasonally moist meadow garden or the damp fringe of a woodland planting, where it can be left undisturbed to naturalize slowly. Because wild populations are restricted and considered locally rare, source only nursery-propagated bulbs rather than wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant the large bulbs 4-6 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in fall in fertile, humus-rich soil that is moist through the growing season; it tolerates summer drying once dormant.

directions: Native to a narrow range in the Wallowa Mountains of northeastern Oregon, this is the largest-bulbed and tallest of the camas species commonly grown, sending up stout stems packed with 30 or more pale blue, star-shaped flowers that open sequentially from the bottom of the raceme upward over several weeks in late spring. The unusually large bulbs make it one of the easier camas species to establish from purchased stock, and it naturalizes readily in a partially shaded woodland-edge or moist meadow setting. Let the strappy foliage die back completely before removing it, since the bulb is recharging for the following spring.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in cool, humus-rich soil that mimics high-elevation coastal forest edges; this rare species is very slow from seed, so purchased bulbs or divisions establish far faster.

directions: Known only from a handful of high-elevation sites in Oregon's northern Coast Range, this fawn lily grows at the interface of open meadows, brushy slopes, and coniferous forest, producing one or two nodding white to pale pink flowers with a bright yellow band at the base of each petal in late spring. It is best suited to a cool, humus-rich woodland-edge planting that stays moist in spring and is shielded from harsh summer sun. Given its critically limited wild range, plant only bulbs or seed obtained from a reputable specialty native-plant source, never wild-collected material.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in light open woodland; it tolerates lean, rocky, serpentine-influenced ground better than many other fawn lilies.

directions: Confined to the Klamath-Siskiyou region of southwestern Oregon and adjacent northern California, often on serpentine-derived soils, this fawn lily bears a pair of broad, mottled leaves and creamy-white flowers with a yellow throat held on short stems above the foliage. It prefers open woodland or shrubby slopes with well-drained soil and light, filtered shade rather than deep cover. Seed-grown plants take several years to reach flowering size, so it rewards patience in a woodland rock garden or native bulb collection where it can be left undisturbed through its long establishment period.
